reading.body:
The four Education & Research AI tools in this data share a common pressure point: student data, and the federal frameworks, FERPA and COPPA, that govern how it can be held and used.

CheggMate, Grammarly for Education, Khanmigo, and Turnitin are all US-jurisdiction products, so the regulatory surface here is narrow and consistent. Three of the four flag FERPA compliance as a concern, and Khanmigo adds COPPA, which applies when the users are children. That concentration of data-privacy notes is the dominant pattern: these tools sit inside institutions that have legal obligations toward students, and the AI layer introduces new ways for those obligations to be tested.

Two tensions are worth noting. Turnitin detects AI-generated writing while the other three tools generate or assist writing, which means institutions may be simultaneously deploying tools on both sides of the same policy question. The data also flags honor code implications for CheggMate and false positive risk for Turnitin, two concerns that point in opposite directions but land on the same student. What the data does not cover is the compute infrastructure behind any of these tools, their model providers, or how inference costs are distributed across institutional licensing.
